newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian beef making good comeback in Japan-AMLC.
newsitem.headline: Australian beef making good comeback in Japan-AMLC.

text.p: Australia's beef exports to its largest market Japan in 1997 are forecast to grow by more than six percent to a total of 300,000 tonnes shipped weight, the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said on Thursday.
Australia's market share of beef imports into Japan had been recovering over the past few months, Samantha Mate of AMLC's Japan marketing programme said in its Meat and Livestock Review.
So far this year Australia's market share had recovered to about 52 percent while that of the U.S. had shrunk to 41 percent, she said.

In 1996 Australia's beef exports to Japan declined for the first time since liberalisation of the Japanese market in 1991 to 280,000 tonnes from the peak of 320,000 tonnes shipped in 1995. The 1996 shipment level gave Australia a Japan market share of 45.4 percent against 49.0 percent for the U.S.

Among many factors behind the reduction were the BSE (mad cow disease) scare, the bacterial infection E.coli, a stronger Australian dollar, a weakening Japanese yen, the over-supply of beef in the U.S. and a subsequent price war in Japan, Mate said.
Growth in forecast Australian beef exports to Japan were despite a continued push by the U.S. of its excess beef into Japan, Mate said.
Japanese concern over the safety of imported beef because of the BSE scare had been reduced as both Australia and the U.S. stressed their BSE-free status, she said.
New country-of-origin packaging regulations in Japan now require that meat retailers indicate the origin of meat.
The AMLC also had been working closely with retailers in Japan to reassure consumers over the E.coli outbreak of last year, she said.
"With improved confidence in the quality and safety of Aussie Beef, sales are expected to recover during 1997."
The recent outbreak of foot and mouth disease in pigs in Taiwan was also likely to shift demand toward Australian beef, she said.
Taiwan, the largest supplier of pork to the Japanese market, exported more than 265,000 tonnes to Japan in 1996, taking more than 40 percent of the imported pork market.
Japan's ban on imports of Taiwan pork from mid-March this year were anticipated to lead to pork shortages when current stocks in Japan were depleted, she said.
With pork the main meat content in processed goods in Japan, the processing sector would have to find another meat source in the event of a shortage in pork supplies.
"Trade sources have indicated that this may lead to greater demand for manufacturing type beef, especially grassfed beef and grainfed trimmings from Australia," she said.
There was also likely to be a shift in demand from pork to beef at retail level.
"With reduced pork supplies, it is likely that the price of pork will increase, making beef more competitively priced," she said.

"The recovery of consumer confidence in beef, coupled with the substitution of pork with beef in the processing, retail and foodservice sectors, all point to an improvement in beef consumption levels in Japan this year," Mate said.
